sections.title: A Pregnant Woman
sections.html:
The mitzva of ona (marital relations) continues to be fulfilled in its regular order throughout all the months of pregnancy, the obligation for most men being twice a week (Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 2:7). Admittedly, in the first months of pregnancy the union may be somewhat difficult for the woman because of nausea and other discomforts; therefore it is necessary to act with greater patience, in order to fulfill the mitzva in the most comfortable manner, but the mitzva remains in place in its full force.

The Sages said that in the last six months, fulfilling the mitzva of ona is also beneficial to the fetus, that it will emerge "whitened" (healthy and vigorous). In the last three months, fulfilling the mitzva of ona is also beneficial for the birth, that it will be easier.1

From the time a woman knows from a medical test that she is pregnant, she no longer has menstrual cycles (vesatot), and therefore her law is that of a "mesuleket damim" (a woman whose bleeding has ceased), who need no longer be concerned about her times of separation (onot perisha). Her law remains so until the end of nursing or until she sees her first veset (menstrual period) (above 6:10).

Sometimes there is bleeding during pregnancy, and then one should turn to a doctor to examine the state of the pregnancy. Halakhically, if it becomes clear that the bleeding is from a wound in the vagina or from the cervix, it does not render her impure. And if the bleeding is from within the uterus, it renders her impure (according to the laws of blood and ketem (bloodstain) explained in chapter 2). However, if it becomes clear with certainty that the bleeding comes from a wound in the uterus unrelated to the pregnancy, it does not render her impure (above 2:14); but as long as the doctor does not determine this with certainty, the bleeding renders her impure.

sections.title: Medical Matters
sections.html:
The Sages said (Berakhot 60a) that in the three months leading up to the birth, it is proper for the couple to pray for the fetus, that it will emerge safely.

Throughout the pregnancy it is a mitzva for the pregnant woman to take special care of her health, for the health of her fetus depends on her health. Included in this, it is a mitzva for her to undergo the tests recommended by the doctors and nurses, which are mostly funded by the health funds in the State of Israel, where public medicine is good. However, there is no need to undergo additional tests, for if the health funds do not fund them, one may assume that they are generally not necessary and are intended for cases of special problems, or for people who are more anxious than is usual. A woman who has supplementary insurance may also undergo the tests that are mostly funded by the supplementary insurance (as explained above 7:6).

Medical examinations do not render the pregnant woman impure. Even stitching the cervix to prevent miscarriage does not render her impure, since this is blood of a wound. In addition, this is not blood coming out of the uterus but from the cervix (above 7:7, n. 7).

From a certain age or in certain situations, there is a medical recommendation to undergo amniocentesis or other tests in order to detect genetic problems in the fetus, and one should act accordingly (Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 9:9).

When it becomes clear that the fetus is very ill or suffers from a severe genetic problem, the poskim disagree as to whether it is desirable, permitted or forbidden to perform an abortion, and the law depends on the severity of the problem and the emotional state of the parents; therefore one should ask a rabbi who is knowledgeable in the field (as explained there in chapter 9, section 8). When the pregnancy involves a risk to the woman's life, all agree that it is a mitzva to perform an abortion in order to save her (ibid. 9:3).

A woman may avail herself of everything the doctors recommend, including an "epidural" to relieve the pains of labor.

When the medical staff recommends inducing labor or performing a cesarean section, out of concern for the welfare of the woman giving birth or concern for the welfare of the fetus, the couple must heed their advice and carry out the induction. If they are apprehensive, as long as a delay is not dangerous, they should request a second medical opinion. But one must not refrain from accepting the medical position for mystical (segula) reasons, such as that changing the time of birth may harm the newborn or the mother. For everything done in order to preserve the life of the woman giving birth or of the fetus is a mitzva and an obligation. And those who act according to segulot and on that account disregard the medical position will have to give an account for not having guarded their lives properly.2

sections.title: From When the Woman Giving Birth Becomes Impure
sections.html:
The birth itself renders her impure: from the time the baby's head or most of its body has emerged, even if no blood came out with it, the woman giving birth becomes impure by Torah law with the impurity of childbirth, one week for the birth of a male and two weeks for the birth of a female (Nidda 28a; SA 194:10; below, section 8).

Often, before the baby emerges, because of the pressure of the labor contractions, blood begins to come out of the uterus, and then the woman giving birth becomes impure. But if, according to the opinion of the doctor or the midwife, the blood came out of the vagina or the cervix, she is pure.

Admittedly, some are stringent and hold that even if the woman giving birth did not see blood, from the time she "sat on the birthstool", that is, when her contractions are strong and frequent and she can no longer walk, she is presumed impure, for there is concern that blood came out and was lost. However, halakhically, only if she actually saw that blood came out of her has she become impure before the birth. Therefore, even after she has lain down on the delivery bed and been examined, if it becomes clear that the birth has not yet begun, as long as she has not seen blood she is pure. And she need not examine herself with an internal bedika (examination); it is enough that she has not seen blood flowing onto her clothes or onto the pad she placed there. And it is preferable that she not examine herself with an internal bedika, so as not to enter into doubt. If she saw a bloodstain that does not render her impure, for example if it was on a colored garment or on a sanitary pad, she is pure. However, if there was a great deal of blood, there is already concern that it is blood from the uterus, and even if it was on a colored garment or a sanitary pad she is impure.3

sections.title: Questions Before the Birth
sections.html:
Dilation check: Often, when the midwife checks the degree of dilation of the cervix before the birth, a small amount of bleeding appears on the glove, which generally results from injury to the cervix, which becomes very sensitive before the birth. Halakhically, when it is clear to the midwife that the source of the blood on the glove is an injury to the cervix, the woman giving birth is pure; and if not, she is impure.

Sometimes before the birth the "waters break"; these are the amniotic fluid that fills the amniotic sac in which the fetus is situated. Sometimes they come out slowly and sometimes all at once. Halakhically, the breaking of the waters does not render her impure, for as long as no blood has come out of the uterus, the woman giving birth is pure.

Mucus plug: Sometimes before the birth the "mucus plug" comes out of the cervix; if it has no blood color, she is pure. And if it has a blood color, some are stringent, out of concern that the blood came out of the uterus into the "mucus plug". And some are lenient and hold that the blood coming out with the plug is considered blood of a wound, which does not render her impure. In practice, those who wish to be lenient may do so.4

Membrane sweep ("stripping") to induce labor: Often the midwife or the doctor performs, at the opening of the uterus, a separation of the membranes from the uterine wall, "stripping", which causes the body to release substances that bring on contractions and advance the birth. Generally this procedure is painful and causes slight bleeding, and therefore some poskim hold that after the separation of the membranes the woman giving birth becomes impure and forbidden. However, halakhically, as long as there is no flow of blood, it is blood that comes out as a result of injury to the uterus caused by this procedure, and therefore it does not render her impure. But if a great deal of blood begins to flow, it is blood that comes out of the uterus because of the contractions, and it renders her impure (see Puah vol. 3, 64:43).

sections.title: The Husband's Assistance to His Wife in Labor
sections.html:
When the woman giving birth has seen blood and become impure, and it is necessary to support her as she gets into the ambulance or walks to the hospital: if there is a woman there who can help her, she should be assisted by her. But if there is no woman there, in a pressing situation the husband may help his wife, since according to the overwhelming majority of the poskim, touching that is not for the sake of pleasure and desire is not forbidden by Torah law but only by rabbinic law, and therefore it is permitted in a pressing situation for the needs of an ill person (above 3:8).

After the woman giving birth has become impure, her husband is forbidden to look at the covered places of her body (above 3:3). Therefore, it is proper to take care that until the birth begins the woman giving birth be covered and the husband stand or sit by her head, so that even when she is examined, the covered places of her body will not be exposed before him. And at the actual moment of birth, when it is not possible to conceal the covered places, those who are stringent are accustomed to leave the room or move to the other side of a curtain, in order to avoid looking at the covered places. And some remain near the woman giving birth, taking care to stand in such a way that they see her face and not the covered places.

In the past, births took place at home, and the midwife together with the women of the family attended to the woman giving birth, while the men, including the husband, did not stand near her, so that the question of whether a husband may attend to his wife in labor did not arise. However, in recent generations birth moved to the hospital, and still, in most traditional families it was accepted that the mother or sister of the woman giving birth would accompany her and attend to her in the delivery room, while the husband waited outside. As the patterns of life changed, and young couples conduct their lives more independently, far from the homes of their mothers and sisters, the husband has often become his wife's main or only companion. And then some hold that during the painful contractions and the birth, when the woman giving birth greatly needs it, her husband may hold her hand and support her. This is because the prohibition of touching that involves no desire is only rabbinic, and in a pressing situation, for the needs of an ill person, one may be lenient.

However, according to many, since there is no necessity that specifically the husband support his wife, one should not be lenient in this. And although those who wish to be lenient have something to rely on, it is proper to be stringent. Only if the woman giving birth enters into severe anxiety and demands that specifically her husband hold her hand and support her, should one be lenient.5

sections.title: The Time of Birth
sections.html:
The state of the marital bond at the time of birth is unique. On the one hand, the woman has no greater partner in her giving birth than her husband; and on the other hand, precisely at the time of birth he is forbidden to touch his wife, since she has become impure and forbidden to him. Perhaps this expresses the greatness of the hour, which is great and awesome, full of majesty and dread. Pain and joy, fear and hope, are intermingled in it. The gate between life and death opens, and a new baby is born, and suddenly he begins to cry, and life, with all its good and bad, begins. A new cycle of hopes and crises and successes opens, and no tangible touch can express the greatness of this awesome hour that touches eternity, for which separation and prayer are fitting. Perhaps this situation can be compared to Yom Kippur, on which, on the one hand, the covenant between husband and wife is revealed, and therefore, when the Temple stood, matches were made on this day. But on the other hand, on this day husband and wife are forbidden to each other. Likewise, on Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol (High Priest) would enter the Holy of Holies on behalf of all Israel, where the value of the love within marriage is expressed, and therefore a Kohen Gadol whose wife had died was unfit for the Yom Kippur service. But on the other hand, the Kohen Gadol had to separate from his wife for seven days before Yom Kippur in order to prepare for the holy service (Yoma 2a). (Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 1:6; Yamim Nora'im 6:12; 9:7; 10:4.)

It is fitting for the woman giving birth to repent before the birth, since the time of birth is a fateful hour involving danger, as the Sages said (Shabbat 31b): "For three transgressions women die at the time of childbirth: for not being careful regarding nidda (menstrual impurity), ḥalla, and the kindling of the [Shabbat] lamp."

It is fitting for the couple to pray that the birth will go well, and that the fetus will emerge healthy and merit a good and long life. And although the medical staff is dedicated and good, it is fitting to remember that birth and health come from God, as the Sages said that the key of childbirth is in God's hands, as are the key of rain and the key of the resurrection of the dead (Ta'anit 2a; Shevet Musar 24).

There is a fine custom that from the time the woman enters the ninth month, her husband is honored in the synagogue with opening the Ark for taking out the Torah scroll and returning it, so that in doing so he will pray for his wife, that God will open her womb and the baby will emerge healthy and whole and illuminate the world with Torah and good deeds (Ḥida, Moreh Be-etzba 3:90).

After the birth it is a mitzva for the woman who gave birth and her husband to thank God with a blessing of thanksgiving: for the birth of a son, "Ha-tov Ve-hametiv" (Who is good and does good), and for the birth of a daughter, "Sheheḥeyanu Ve-kiyemanu Ve-higi'anu La-zman Ha-zeh" (Who has given us life, sustained us and brought us to this time) (see Peninei Halakha: Berakhot 17:13, n. 11).

sections.title: Birth on Shabbat
sections.html:
A woman giving birth is considered an ill person whose life is in danger; therefore, when according to medical instruction she must get to a hospital, she should be driven to the hospital even on Shabbat, in the way one usually travels on a weekday.

Carrying in a place without an eruv: Everything that must be taken for the medical care of the woman giving birth may be taken from the house to the car even in a place without an eruv. This includes necessary medications, medical documents and an identity card. Things that are important to the woman giving birth but are not essential for her medical care, such as extra clothes, food and books, may be taken in a place without an eruv in an unusual manner (be-shinui), and they should walk continuously from the house until they place them inside the car.

Bringing muktze items: As a rule it is forbidden to take items that are muktze, but when it is known that on Motza'ei Shabbat there will be great need for muktze items, such as money and a mobile phone, it is permitted to put them into the bag in an unusual manner and bring them to the hospital incidentally with the bag. When the woman giving birth must be rushed to the hospital quickly and there is no time to think about the methods of carrying, one may take all the necessary things, even those that are muktze, without making an effort to do so in an unusual manner. If the muktze items were lying in the bag together with necessary things, even though there is no great need for them, it is permitted to bring the bag with them inside it. Therefore, it is good to prepare the bag before Shabbat (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 27:6).

A nearby hospital: One should travel to the nearest hospital, so as not to add to the desecration of Shabbat unnecessarily. Even when the woman giving birth prefers the more distant hospital because it is considered more professional, or because it is run according to halakha, it is forbidden to travel to it on Shabbat, since this is not a medical consideration involving pikuaḥ nefesh (danger to life). For if it were a matter of pikuaḥ nefesh, then even on a weekday women giving birth who live in the north or south of the country would be directed to travel to the best hospitals in the center of the country. However, if reaching the preferred hospital requires lengthening the route only a little, this is included among the things done to set the mind of the woman giving birth at ease. All this is in a normal situation, but when there is a special need, such as a woman giving birth who is at special risk and for whom a treatment plan has already been set at the distant hospital, it is permitted to travel to it on Shabbat even when it is much further away. Everything is according to the accepted medical guidance: the more complex and difficult the case, the more it is permitted to lengthen the route for it (see Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 27:7).

Travel of the companion: The woman giving birth needs a companion to come with her, in order to attend to her and to make sure that even at times of heavy workload the medical staff treats her as necessary. But since there is no need for more than one companion, it is forbidden for two companions to travel with her. A birth companion (doula), too, is not needed at the level of pikuaḥ nefesh, and therefore, if there is already one companion, such as the husband or the mother of the woman giving birth, the birth companion may not travel on Shabbat. Only in exceptional cases, when the woman giving birth becomes hysterical and demands that both her husband and her mother travel with her, may both travel. Likewise, if out of severe anxiety she demands that the birth companion be called, one may accede to her request. But it is forbidden to plan in advance that more than one companion will travel with her on Shabbat. And if the journey is long and they are traveling in a private car and the husband intends to drive, they may bring along the birth companion or the mother, because sometimes there is a need for an additional person to give prompt help to the woman giving birth during the journey.6

sections.title: The Impurity of the Woman After Childbirth and Her Purification
sections.html:
As we have learned (in section 3), the birth itself renders her impure: if she gave birth to a male, her impurity lasts seven days, and after that she has thirty-three days of purity. And if she gave birth to a female, her impurity lasts two weeks, and after that she has sixty-six days of purity. That is, by Torah law the woman who gave birth may immerse and become pure from the impurity of her childbirth after one week for a male and two weeks for a female, even if bleeding from her uterus still continues. For all the blood that comes out of her until the end of the fortieth day for a male and until the end of the eightieth day for a female is "dam tohar" (blood of purity), that is, blood that does not render her impure to her husband. However, throughout the forty days for a woman who gave birth to a male and the eighty days for a woman who gave birth to a female, she is forbidden to go up to the Temple and to eat of the sacrifices, and if she is a kohen's wife or daughter she is forbidden to eat teruma and ḥalla anywhere in the land. After the end of the days of purity, the woman who gave birth returns to the regular law of every woman, and it is a mitzva for her to go up to the Temple and bring an ola (burnt offering) to give thanks for the birth, and a ḥatat (sin offering) to cleanse herself of the deficiencies that clung to her in her giving birth. As it is stated (Vayikra 12:1-8): "When a woman conceives and gives birth to a male, she shall be impure seven days; as in the days of her menstrual separation she shall be impure. On the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised. Then she shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of purity; she shall not touch any holy thing, nor come into the Sanctuary, until the days of her purification are completed. But if she gives birth to a female, she shall be impure two weeks, as in her separation; and she shall remain sixty-six days in the blood of purity. When the days of her purification are completed, for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring a lamb in its first year for a burnt offering, and a young pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering, to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, to the kohen. He shall offer it before the Lord and make atonement for her, and she shall be purified from the source of her blood; this is the law for her who gives birth, to a male or to a female. And if she cannot afford a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering; and the kohen shall make atonement for her, and she shall be pure."

One may say that the difference between the law of a woman who gave birth to a male and one who gave birth to a female is that with a woman who gave birth to a male, the impurity and the rectification are more revealed: the impurity is expressed in the foreskin, and the rectification in the brit mila (circumcision), and the whole process is shorter. Whereas with a woman who gave birth to a female, the impurity and the purification are more hidden and deeper, and therefore they last twice as long.

In practice, the daughters of Israel took upon themselves to regard every drop of blood as a sighting of a "zava" and to sit shiv'a neki'im (seven clean days) for it, and their custom was accepted by the Sages as established halakha (above 1:6-7). Following this, all Israel took upon themselves to regard "dam tohar" too as impure blood after the sighting of which one must sit seven clean days, and this was established as halakha. Therefore, only after the bleeding following the birth has ended should the woman who gave birth perform a hefsek tahara (examination establishing the cessation of bleeding), count seven clean days and immerse. Likewise, if after she has become pure she again sees blood during the days of purity, she becomes impure from it, and after the bleeding stops she should perform a hefsek tahara, count seven clean days, and immerse again for her purification. (If a rare case occurred in which a woman who gave birth to a female managed to complete seven clean days before the end of two weeks from her giving birth, she should wait until the end of the two weeks and only then immerse.)

A woman who gives birth by cesarean section does not become impure with the impurity of childbirth and has no days of dam tohar (Nidda 40a). But since in practice after the birth blood comes out of the uterus through the vagina, she becomes impure from it like the other laws of nidda, and after she performs a hefsek tahara and counts seven clean days, she should immerse and become pure.7

sections.title: The Meaning of the Impurity of Childbirth
sections.html:
In every descent of a great idea into the world there is a certain aspect of death. So it was in the creation of the world, as it is stated (Bereshit 1:3): "And God said: Let there be light, and there was light." The Sages explained that the idea was that there be a great light, but in practice, because of the deficiencies in the world, so that the wicked would not benefit from the great light and use it for evil, the great light was diminished and contracted as it descended into the world, for the expression "va-yehi" ("and there was") alludes to sorrow (Zohar I 30b; 31b, and elsewhere). However, the descent is for the sake of ascent, and after the process of rectification is completed, the word of God will stand, and the great light will be revealed and will even be intensified by the additional blessing that the created beings will bestow upon it. Similarly, every vision is at its beginning incomparably greater than its realization, and only after a long process of rectification is the vision fully realized, and even more.

So too in every birth, the hopes are infinite; the heart tends to believe that after the miracle of birth the whole world will change for the better, and the new child will be perfect, wonderful and happy, wise and healthy, and in his days the redeemer will come. In practice, after the birth one falls into the routine of life, into the pains and the exhaustion. The baby too will have to cope with challenges and crises like all human beings. The body of the woman who gave birth also feels this; this is the particular low mood that many women feel in the period after giving birth.

The impurity that accompanies birth expresses the sorrow over the hopes and dreams that will not be realized. In the days of impurity, which contain a kind of mourning over the fall of the vision to the ground of reality, the woman who gave birth can come to terms with the deficiencies of reality, receive her child with joy, gird herself with strength and vitality to cope with the challenges that will accompany raising and educating him, and derive deep satisfaction from the wonderful privilege, than which there is none higher, of being a "mother". A similar process is undergone in these days by the father, during which he must stand to the side and help his wife rest as much as possible, and in the course of this absorb the great role that has fallen to his lot, of being a "father".

In the first stage the impurity is more severe, and it expresses the mother's emptying of her dreams, and the fall of the fetus from the wondrous world in which it was in its mother's womb into this world with all its sorrow and weeping. In the second stage, of "dam tohar", the impurity is less severe, and it expresses the intermediate state, in which life gains strength together with the recognition that it is accompanied by difficulties and crises, and that only through coping with them can one progress toward the realization of all the dreams. Therefore at this stage, by Torah law the woman is not forbidden to her husband, but she is forbidden to touch holy things and to enter the Temple. And according to the custom of Israel, if she sees blood during these days, she becomes impure as a nidda.

As a continuation of the meaning of the laws of impurity, the woman who gave birth and her family must pay attention to her physical and emotional state and create comfortable conditions for her to rest, so that the woman who gave birth will sleep as much as possible, through which she can recover quickly; and without it, the low mood common in the period after birth may, God forbid, turn into depression. When the woman who gave birth suffers from a low mood that does not pass, one should turn to a family doctor in order to receive mild medications to ease the low mood and prevent deterioration, in addition to receiving encouragement and help from the family in order to add hours of sleep. In a more severe state of "postpartum depression", there is an obligation to make use of strong medications given by a psychiatrist (who can be reached through the health fund), in order to cure the depression and prevent a deterioration that may turn into a permanent condition of depressive illness and even reach mortal danger. In this situation one must not delay or make do with alternative treatments, since this is a dangerous illness.

sections.title: After a Miscarriage
sections.html:
A woman who miscarried a fetus whose limbs had not yet had time to form, that is, within forty days from conception, does not become impure with the impurity of childbirth but only with the impurity of nidda. Therefore, when the bleeding stops she should perform a hefsek tahara, count seven clean days and immerse for her purification.

If the miscarriage occurred after the fetus's limbs had already formed, that is, after the fetus had reached the stage of development of forty days from conception, the miscarriage renders her impure with the impurity of childbirth. If the fetus was male, her impurity is one week, and if female, two weeks. When there is doubt whether the fetus was female, as often happens, her impurity lasts two weeks. Then, at the earliest, she should perform a hefsek tahara after seven days, so that in practice the tevila will be after two weeks (SA 194:3). However, generally after a miscarriage at such a stage the bleeding continues for more than a week, so that in any case it is not possible to become pure before two weeks have passed.8

Shabbat is desecrated in order to save a fetus in its mother's womb, even when it is less than forty days old (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 27:3).

A baby who was born with problems and died within thirty days of his birth: some say that there is no mitzva to bury him, since he is considered a nefel (non-viable infant) and there is no mitzva to bury nefalim (Or Zaru'a; SA OḤ 526:9-10). And some say that it is a mitzva to bury nefalim, and even if the fetus was born several months before its time, if it has human form, it is a mitzva to bury it (Magen Avraham 526:20; Sho'el U-meshiv Telita'ah 1:15). The custom is to be stringent and to bury a fetus that has form, through the "Ḥevra Kaddisha" (burial society), without the participation of the parents, in order to spare them unnecessary sorrow.9

Often, after a natural miscarriage has occurred, the medical recommendation is to perform a "curettage" of the remains of the pregnancy, in order to ensure the healing of the uterus. Without this, the bleeding sometimes continues for a longer time, and the woman will not succeed in becoming pregnant in the future.

The laws of mourning do not apply to the death of fetuses; however, the loss may be accompanied by great sorrow, and then the couple should recite the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, the true Judge" (Dayan Ha-emet). One may recite the blessing and the other answer Amen (see Peninei Halakha: Berakhot 17:8).
